lead: A tool does not cut forever. Heat, friction and rubbing wear the cutting edge, and wear grows faster as speed rises. Tool life is the cutting time before wear reaches a set limit. Taylor's equation links speed and life with a power law. Machinability ranks materials by how easily they cut. These ideas set cutting speed, feed and depth of cut on a lathe or milling machine, so a shop gets the most parts per edge without scrapping the job.
prereq: You need: cutting forces from 5.2 and tool materials from 5.4.

blocks.text: Two faces of a single-point tool wear. The flank face rubs the new surface; flank wear VB is the average width of the wear land, in mm. The rake face carries the chip; crater wear is a hollow on the rake face, measured as depth KT in mm. Notch wear appears at the depth-of-cut line. Chipping is small fracture of the edge. A built-up edge (BUE) is chip material welded to the edge; when it breaks away it pulls tool particles and leaves a rough finish.

items: Abrasion: hard inclusions in the work scratch the tool; strong at low speed.
Adhesion: hot metal welds to the tool and tears off, taking tool material.
Diffusion: atoms move from tool to chip at high temperature.
Oxidation: the hot edge reacts with air.

blocks.text: Tool life T is the cutting time in minutes before the tool stops meeting the criterion. A common ISO-style limit is average flank wear VB = 0.3 mm, with maximum 0.6 mm. Surface finish, chatter or spindle power may end life earlier. A worn tool raises cutting force and temperature, so the last minutes of life are costly.
Taylor's equation links cutting speed and tool life by a power law. It is used to choose a speed for a wanted life, or to predict life after a speed change.

blocks.where: V is cutting speed in m/min; T is tool life in min; n is the tool-life exponent; C is a constant for the tool-work pair.

blocks.text: Taking logs gives log V + n log T = log C, a straight line on log-log axes. Typical n is about 0.1 for high-speed steel (HSS), 0.2 to 0.3 for carbide, and 0.4 to 0.6 for ceramic. C is the speed that gives T = 1 min, so C carries units that depend on n. With n = 0.25, doubling V divides T by 2⁴ = 16. A carbide tool that lasts 40 min at 120 m/min lasts only about 2.5 min at 240 m/min. High-n ceramics tolerate speed better; that is why they run fast on cast iron and nickel alloys.

Machinability is how easily a material cuts. A material with good machinability gives low cutting force, long tool life, good surface finish and short broken chips. The machinability index compares a material with free-cutting steel, taken as 100%. A higher index means easier cutting. Ductile metals build a BUE; hard inclusions abrade the tool; low thermal conductivity keeps heat at the edge and speeds diffusion wear.

blocks.where: MRR is material removal rate in mm³/min; v is cutting speed in m/min; f is feed in mm/rev; d is depth of cut in mm. If v is in mm/min, MRR = v f d.

blocks.text: Cutting speed has the strongest effect on tool life. Feed and depth of cut raise chip area, force and MRR, but too much feed spoils finish and too much depth can cause chatter. A shop first picks v from Taylor's equation for the life it wants, then picks f and d within finish and power limits.

figure.caption: Tool life falls sharply as cutting speed rises on the Taylor curve; at 120 m/min the curve reads about 39 min.

spec.aria: A curve falls steeply from about 81 minutes at 100 m/min to about 5 minutes at 200 m/min, showing tool life dropping as speed rises.

examples.question: A carbide tool follows Taylor's equation V T^0.25 = 300, with V in m/min and T in min. (a) Find tool life at V = 120 m/min. (b) Find tool life at V = 240 m/min. (c) Find the cutting speed for T = 60 min.
examples.answer: Tool life is about 39.1 min at 120 m/min, about 2.44 min at 240 m/min, and the speed for 60 min life is about 107.8 m/min.

traps: Taylor exponent n is positive. A negative n turns the falling tool-life curve into a rising one.
C is not a fixed speed for all tools; its value and unit depend on n. Do not compare C values when n differs.
Tool life falls as a power law, not linearly with cutting speed. A small speed rise can cut life many times.
Average flank wear 0.3 mm and maximum 0.6 mm are criteria, not universal death of the tool; surface finish may fail earlier.
Crater wear is on the rake face; flank wear is on the flank face. Do not swap the two in a diagram.

quiz.q: Define flank wear and crater wear on a single-point tool.
quiz.a: Flank wear is the wear land on the flank face, measured as average width VB in mm. Crater wear is a hollow on the rake face, measured as depth KT in mm.

quiz.q: Why does doubling cutting speed reduce tool life by much more than half?
quiz.a: Taylor's equation gives T proportional to V^(-1/n). Since n is less than 1, the exponent 1/n is greater than 1. Doubling V divides T by 2^(1/n), which is 16 when n = 0.25.

quiz.q: A tool follows V T^0.2 = 400, with V in m/min and T in min. Find tool life at V = 150 m/min.
A built-up edge forms during cutting. Explain whether it protects or harms the tool.
quiz.a: A BUE can shield the edge briefly, but it is unstable. When it breaks away it pulls tool particles, raises cutting force and leaves a rough surface, so it is not a reliable protection.

quiz.q: In turning, v = 120 m/min, f = 0.2 mm/rev and d = 1.5 mm. Find MRR.
quiz.a: MRR = 1000 v f d = 1000 × 120 × 0.2 × 1.5 = 36,000 mm³/min, which is 36 cm³/min.

quiz.q: What does a machinability index of 120 mean?
quiz.a: It means the material is easier to cut than free-cutting steel taken as 100. At the same conditions it gives longer tool life, lower force or better finish, or it can be cut at a higher speed for the same life.

quiz.q: Why do ceramic tools have a higher Taylor exponent n than HSS tools?
quiz.a: Ceramics keep hardness at higher cutting temperature, so diffusion and oxidation wear start at higher speed. Their life is less sensitive to speed, which appears as a larger n in V Tⁿ = C.

beyond: Not for the exam. Shops use tool-life data to set speed tables and to schedule edge changes before a batch is scrapped. Modern CNC machines estimate tool wear from spindle load and acoustic emission, and adapt feed and speed in real time. Coatings such as TiN and Al₂O₃ slow diffusion and oxidation, which shifts the Taylor constants. Search next for tool condition monitoring, ISO tool-life testing, and machinability of titanium and nickel alloys.
